“Story!”

He seemed deliberately to misunderstand the word she had repeated, for he hurried on: “Yes, customers. In banking, that's what we generally call the people we deal with. He was a French gentleman, a man of science, a highly educated man—a doctor.”

“Not from Beauvais?”

“Yes, from Beauvais. Like Monsieur Manette, your father, this gentleman came from Beauvais. Like Monsieur Manette, your father, he had a good reputation in Paris. I had the honor of knowing him there. Our dealings were professional, but confidential. At that time I worked at our French branch and had been there—oh, twenty years.”

“At that time—may I ask when you mean, sir?”

“I'm speaking of twenty years ago, miss. He married an English lady, and I was one of the trustees managing his affairs. Like many other French gentlemen and families, he left all his business in Tellson's hands. In much the same way, I am, or have been, a trustee of one sort or another for scores of our customers. These are simply business relationships, miss. There's no friendship in them, no special interest, nothing emotional. Throughout my working life I've passed from one to the next, just as I pass from one customer to another in my working day. In short, I have no feelings. I'm merely a machine. To continue—”

“But this is my father's story, sir. And I'm beginning to think”—her forehead, with its curious furrows, showed how intently she watched him—“that when I became an orphan, after my mother outlived my father by only two years, you were the person who brought me to England. I'm almost certain it was you.”

Mr. Lorry took the small hand she hesitantly held out in trust to grasp his, and raised it rather formally to his lips. Then he immediately led the young lady back to her chair. Holding its back with his left hand, he used his right now to rub his chin, now to tug at his wig beside his ears, now to emphasize his words. He stood looking down at her face while she looked up at his.

“Miss Manette, it was me. And you'll understand how truthful I was when I said I had no feelings and all my relationships were purely business, when you remember that I haven't seen you since. No; Tellson's has been your guardian all this time, and I've been occupied with Tellson's other affairs. Feelings! I have no time for them, no opportunity. I spend my whole life, miss, turning the handle of an enormous money machine.”

“But in fact, once we have risen to any particular altitude, the measurable mass of air we pass through in a further ascent is by no means proportional to the additional height gained, as the earlier discussion makes clear. Instead, that proportion continually decreases. Evidently, then, however high we climb, we cannot literally reach a boundary beyond which no atmosphere exists. It must still be there, I reasoned, even if it has become infinitely thin.

“I knew, on the other hand, that arguments had been advanced for a definite outer boundary to the atmosphere, beyond which there is absolutely no air. Yet those who supported this boundary had overlooked a circumstance which, although it did not conclusively disprove their position, seemed to me to deserve serious investigation. Compare the intervals between successive arrivals of Encke's comet at perihelion, allowing as precisely as possible for every disturbance caused by the gravitational pull of the planets: those intervals appear to be gradually shortening. In other words, the major axis of the comet's elliptical orbit is becoming shorter, slowly but with perfect regularity. That is exactly what we should expect if the comet encountered resistance from an extremely thin ethereal medium spread throughout the region of its orbit. Such a medium would clearly reduce the comet's speed, increasing its centripetal force by weakening its centrifugal force. Put another way, the sun's attraction would steadily gain the advantage, drawing the comet closer with every revolution. Indeed, no other explanation accounts for this change. Furthermore, the actual diameter of the same comet's surrounding cloud visibly contracts rapidly as it approaches the sun, and expands just as rapidly as it moves away towards aphelion. Wasn't I justified in agreeing with M. Valz that this apparent reduction in volume results from compression by the ethereal medium already mentioned, which becomes denser the nearer it is to the sun? The lens-shaped phenomenon known as the zodiacal light also deserved attention. This glow, so clearly visible in the tropics and impossible to confuse with the light of a meteor, rises diagonally from the horizon and generally follows the direction of the sun's equator. To me, it plainly resembled a thin atmosphere extending out from the sun to at least beyond the orbit of Venus, and, I believed, indefinitely farther. Indeed, I could not suppose that this medium was restricted to the course of the comet's elliptical orbit or to the sun's immediate neighborhood.

“April 19. This morning, around nine, with the moon's surface terrifyingly close and my anxiety at its highest, the pump of my condenser finally showed clear signs of a change in the atmosphere. This brought me enormous relief. By ten, I had reason to think its density had increased substantially. By eleven, the equipment required very little effort to operate. At noon, after some hesitation, I risked unscrewing the tourniquet. When this caused no discomfort, I finally opened the rubber chamber completely and detached it from around the basket. As might have been expected, such a reckless and dangerous experiment immediately produced spasms and a severe headache. Yet these symptoms and the other breathing difficulties were not severe enough to threaten my life, and I resolved to endure them as well as I could. Every moment of my approach to the denser layers near the moon would carry me farther beyond them. My descent, however, was still extraordinarily violent. It soon became alarmingly clear that, although I had probably been right to expect an atmosphere with a density proportional to the satellite's mass, I had been mistaken in thinking that even its surface density could support the great weight in my balloon's basket. Yet it should have supported that weight as effectively as the atmosphere at the earth's surface, assuming that actual gravity on either planet was proportional to the density of its atmosphere. My headlong fall gave ample proof that this was not so. Why it was not can be explained only by reference to the possible geological disturbances I mentioned earlier. Whatever the reason, I was now very close to the planet, plunging towards it with terrifying speed. Without losing a moment, I threw overboard first my ballast, then my water barrels, then my condenser and rubber chamber, and finally every object in the basket. It was useless. I continued falling at a horrifying rate and was now less than half a mile above the surface. As a last resort, I discarded my coat, hat, and boots and cut away the basket itself, which weighed a considerable amount. Clinging to the netting with both hands, I had just enough time to notice that the countryside, as far as I could see, was densely dotted with tiny dwellings. Then I tumbled headfirst into the very center of a fantastical-looking city, landing amid an enormous crowd of ugly little people. Not one spoke a word or made the slightest effort to help me. They simply stood like a collection of idiots, grinning absurdly, their hands on their hips, and casting sidelong looks at me and my balloon.
